The five English versions split on diKita: KJV/ASV 'thou hast broken', YLT 'bruised', BBE 'broken'. The root is dkh/dk', 'to crush'; I chose 'crushed' for both layers, the stronger of the two.

agent_notes: tismekheni is 3fs ('it will sustain me'), so the 'willing spirit' is the subject, not the object as in KJV 'uphold me with'. Ibn Ezra and Radak discuss this feminine verb explicitly. YLT keeps the subject reading; KJV, ASV and Webster turn it into an instrument. I follow the grammar in the literal layer and the instrumental sense in the dramatic layer.

nediva can mean 'willing', 'generous' or 'noble'. Rashi takes it as nobility/princeliness (qetsinut), Metzudat Zion as generosity, Radak as the willing spirit of the poet. I kept 'willing' in the literal layer and named the range in the commentary.

damim (plural) is 'bloods' idiomatically, meaning bloodshed or blood-guilt. The 'Uriah' reading comes from the superscription and the commentators (Rashi, Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri), not from the verse. The 1 Kings framing aside, I note the Ibn Ezra view that this is not murder in the legal sense.

agent_notes: Reviewer request addressed: the earlier commentary misquoted the KJV. It now quotes KJV 51:16 exactly ('thou desirest not sacrifice … thou delightest not in burnt offering') and ASV ('delightest not in sacrifice … no pleasure in burnt-offering'), and states the real point: the Hebrew pair chafetz / ratzah is one parallel pair, and the English versions spread 'desire / delight / pleasure' across it differently, so a reader cannot see that the two verbs are near-synonyms.

וְאֶתֵּנָה is a cohortative with the volitive ה (first person, 'let me give / I would give'). STEPBible's 'and I will give [it]' is future; I glossed it as 'and I would give [it]' because the clause is conditional-contrary in sense ('else would I give it', KJV). Rashi on this verse reads it the same way ('if you desired, I would give it to you').

The claim that sacrifice does not cover deliberate sin rests on Rashi, Radak and Meiri in the packet; the Torah's sin-offering is for inadvertent sin (Lev 4), which I cite only as background and have not quoted. The verse's own text does not name David's sin.

agent_notes: chololti (H2342) is glossed 'I was brought forth' by STEPBible. The verb is a Polal of chil/chul, 'to writhe, to bear in labor', which can mean 'to be born' (Ps 51:7; Isa 51:2 per Metzudat Zion) or 'to be formed'. The KJV's 'shapen' leans on the Vulgate-era 'formed'. I kept 'was brought forth in labor' / 'was born' and did not build the doctrine of original sin into the translation: Meiri, Radak and Malbim read it as hyperbole or as the nature of human desire, not as inherited guilt.

tuchot (H2910) occurs only here and in Job 38:36, and its meaning is disputed. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion say 'kidneys, covered in fat' (from tuach, 'to smear over'); Rashi also offers 'extent' (from a root linked to mitchavei qeshet). Modern lexica (HALOT) take it as 'inward parts' by the same reasoning. I rendered 'the plastered-over places' in the literal layer and 'inward parts' in the dramatic one, and flagged the uncertainty.

agent_notes: STEPBible glosses techate'eni as 'you will cleanse from sin me'. It is a Piel of chata' ('to sin'), privative: 'to un-sin, to purify from sin'. The verb forms in vv. 9-10 are imperfects with a jussive-like sense and not plain futures; the KJV 'Purge me ... and I shall be clean' is therefore defensible, but the Hebrew has no imperative.
